Responsiveness

Source: vignettes/articles/responsiveness.Rmd
responsiveness.Rmd

A Shiny app can feel slow where a JavaScript app does not: a click, a pause, then the page changes. This article says where a Shiny app waits, why, and what this package does about each part – so that the page answers at once while the server keeps the data. Performance is about the other kind of slowness, a page taking long to start.

Where a Shiny app waits

Shiny is driven by the server. The browser reports every change – a click, a key, a selection – over a WebSocket; R runs the observers and outputs that depend on it; the result travels back and the page is changed. Almost all state lives in R, even state only the page needs, such as whether a dialog is open.

That design is what makes Shiny easy: one language, reactive state, no API to write. Its costs come in four kinds, and only some of them are the design’s own:

The wait Why Shiny’s design?
A click answered after a pause Every interaction is a round trip: the network, then R Yes: the state is on the server
One user’s work stops the others An R process serves many sessions, one thing at a time Partly: R is single-threaded; the round trips make every user meet it
Updates that cost more than they change renderUI() sends a whole piece of page again, which the browser takes down and builds again No: a way of sending, not the design
A computation that takes long The data, the model No: the same in any framework

The first is the one users see most. A JavaScript application (Vue, React) splits the work differently: what only the page needs – a dialog open, a size picked, the tab shown – stays in the browser and costs nothing, and the backend is asked only for data and decisions.

What the package does

The package keeps Shiny’s way – R decides, inputs and outputs are reactive – and adds the browser’s way where it serves. Four parts, one for each kind of wait.

1. The page’s state stays in the page

A component’s argument given v_bind()/v_model() follows state in the browser, with no round trip:

el_radio_group(
  "size",
  choices = c("large", "default", "small"),
  selected = "default"
)
el_space(size = v_bind("$inputs.size"), el_card("One"), el_card("Two"))

vue_store("ui", state = list(open = FALSE))
el_button("open", "Open", on = list(click = "$vueStore.ui.open = true"))
el_dialog(
  "tips",
  title = "Tips",
  visible = v_model("$vueStore.ui.open"),
  content = "Opened in the browser."
)
Tips
Opened in the browser.

$inputs.<id> is another component’s value; a vue_store() is state several components share, both ways – closing the dialog sets the store back. An on handler acts in the browser too: setting a store, or showing Element’s message, "$message('Saved')". The server still hears every input$<id>, and can still update a bound field. See the Shiny guide’s “Linking components in the browser”.

Measured on this package’s development server (headless Chrome, the app on the same machine, so with no network in the way), the time from a click to a dialog on screen:

The dialog opened R idle R busy for 2 s with another click
by the server, update_el_dialog() 64 ms 1,822 ms
in the browser, v_bind()/v_model() 1.4 ms 1.2 ms

Over a real network the first row adds the network’s round trip; the second row does not change. And the busy column is the second kind of wait made visible: the server’s dialog waits for R to be free, the browser’s does not ask it.

2. Little crosses the wire

When the server must be asked, the package sends as little as it can:

  • Changes, not pages. A component an output renders a second time gets only the data fields that changed (render_vue(), render_el_table()): no markup, no new Vue app, the user’s sort and open rows kept. A table or calendar changed row by row gets only those rows (update_el_table(insert =, replace =, delete =)).
  • One message per flush. Updates and method calls are queued and sent together when Shiny flushes, as Shiny’s own update*Input()s are.
  • Only the events asked for. A component reports its value and the user’s deliberate actions; Element’s other events only with events =. A typed value can be debounced with rate.
  • Cached for everyone. render_vue(), render_vue_data() and render_el_table() work with bindCache(): a render shared by every session, each page still sent only what it lacks.
  • Only what is seen. A tree loads a node’s children when it opens (lazy = TRUE); el_table_v2() draws the rows in view; a select can draw its options when opened (persistent = FALSE).

3. The page does not wait blind

  • Changed at once, confirmed after. An editable table cell takes the new value in the browser as it is typed, and the server converts it to the column’s type afterwards – an optimistic update.
  • Waiting shown where it happens. el_table_output() covers a table with Element’s mask while Shiny recalculates it (loading); templates read $recalculating.<id> and $busy; el_page() covers the page until every component is drawn.

4. One user’s work does not stop the others

R does one thing at a time per process, so a long computation in one session holds up every session in it. Shiny’s ExtendedTask, with promises or mirai, runs it elsewhere, and every render function of this package waits for a promise. el_button(task = TRUE), bound with bslib::bind_task_button(), is a button for such a task, busy while it runs, as bslib’s own task button is:

ui <- el_page(
  el_button("go", "Fit the model", task = TRUE),
  el_table_output("fit")
)
server <- function(input, output, session) {
  fit <- ExtendedTask$new(function(data) {
    mirai::mirai(
      as.data.frame(coef(summary(lm(mpg ~ wt + hp, data = data)))),
      data = data
    )
  })
  bslib::bind_task_button(fit, "go")
  observeEvent(input$go, fit$invoke(mtcars))
  output$fit <- render_el_table(el_table(data = fit$result(), rownames = TRUE))
}

Where each thing goes

It is Put it With
The page’s own state: open, picked, shown the browser v_bind()/v_model(), vue_store(), on
A message about what the page did the browser on = list(click = "$message(...)")
Data, and what is computed from it the server outputs, update_*()
A decision that matters: who may see what, what is saved the server observers; the browser’s state is a convenience, never a permission
A long computation another process ExtendedTask with mirai or promises

The two halves meet in input$<id>: whatever the page does, the server can see it, and whatever the server decides, it can set on the page.
